As far as I have understood, these decree laws were amended by the competent assembly, by the legislative assembly. As a result, were these two texts not amended subsequently in the course of 1992 or in 1993 or in 1994? Could the Defence clarify this because thanks to you we found out that the decree laws -- some of the decree laws were subsequently amended, and hence the question concerning these two documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at a time of imminent threat of war and at a time of war, as witnesses have testified, and because of the encirclement of Sarajevo, it was impossible for parliament to hold session. The Presidency had the role of the parliament. And in 1992 and in 1993, they issued decree laws. In accordance with the constitution, when the parliament is in session, the Presidency had the obligation of confirming these decrees as law; this happened later in 1994 and in 1995 when these decrees were probably confirmed by the parliament. But in 1992 and 1993 and 1994, they were in fact laws which were obeyed by all the organs as well as by the courts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. With regard to this legal issue, are there any comments that the Prosecution would like to make? Defence counsel has told us given the state of war in 1992, the parliament could not hold sessions and these -- the texts were issued as decree laws and perhaps at a subsequent date, but Defence can't provide us with more information, subsequently texts were completely ratified or may have been completely ratified. What is Defence's [as interpreted] position, legal position?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we were planning to take one hour, but I would like to ask the Trial Chamber for leave to examine the witness for an hour and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You need an hour and 15 minutes; that is not a problem. But it's important for us to conclude by 1.45, because as you know, there's an afternoon session and we can't work beyond that time. It's absolutely necessary to finish by that time. I'd also like to point out to the Defence that sometimes there are questions that are interesting but that might not be asked, questions about his education, et cetera. These are not indispensable questions, perhaps. So please try to focus on essential issues so everyone can understand the witness's testimony and ensure that his testimony is useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir, I would first like to make sure that you can hear what I'm saying in your own language. If so, please say yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you have been called here as a witness for General Hadzihasanovic's Defence. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names and date of birth. It appears that there is a delay with the interpretation. Have you heard my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've understood the question. My name is Asim Delalic. I was born on the 10th of December, 1955.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which town or village were you born in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was born in the village of Suhi Dol in the municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently employed; and if so, what is your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm currently employed. I work as a graphic artist. I work in the printing company called Borastani [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993 did you hold a military position; if so, what sort of military position and which unit were you assigned to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1992 and 1993 I was first in a detachment in the Mehurici detachment, and when the 306th Mountain Brigade was formed, I was a member of that brigade. I was in the Mehurici detachment as a commander in the detachment of military police, and then I was an assistant commander for security. And in the 306th Mountain Brigade I was the assistant commander for security from the time that the brigade was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So have you already testified before a national or an international court with regard to the events that took place in your country or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I would like to provide you with some information concerning the procedure that we'll be following here. You'll first have to answer questions that will be put to you by General Hadzihasanovic's Defence, whom you have already met when you were being proofed. Defence counsel have told us that they will need about one hour and 15 minutes for your examination-in-chief. Once they have completed their examination-in-chief, the Prosecution, to your right, will conduct their cross-examination, which will also take one hour and 15 minutes. Then the Defence may put additional questions to you. And then the three Judges sitting before you, if they believe it is necessary, may also ask you questions. I would also like to point out two other things to you. You have just taken the solemn declaration, which means that you should not give false testimony. And secondly, and this is a procedural matter, if a witness believes that his answer could be used against him at a subsequent date, if he believes his answer could be used to prosecute him, the witness may refuse to answer the question. This is a situation we have never encountered so far, but if such a situation should arise, the Chamber can compel the witness to answer the question but the Chamber guarantees the witness a form if immunity in that case. Try to answer the questions to the best of your ability and if you find that a question is complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it. Please inform us of any difficulties you may run into. We will be having two 25-minute breaks. The first break will be at about 10.30 and the second break will be about 12.30. Usually if everything proceeds smoothly, we should be able to complete your examination today and you should then be able to return to your country. Without wasting any more time, I will give the floor to Defence counsel now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Delalic. You said that you were a graphic artist, a graphic designer by profession. Tell me, did you have any military education before the war?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Before the war I had no professional military education, apart from the fact that I was in the JNA and I was in charge of the military police detachment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from the Trial Chamber you said that when the 306th Mountain Brigade was formed you became assistant commander for security. Tell me, in the course of 1993 what sort of duties did you perform?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1993 I worked as the assistant commander for security. I had no other duties --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said that he was a lance corporal in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since the Trial Chamber has already heard a lot about the formation of the 306th Mountain Brigade, my question for you is as follows: When the 306th was formed, did any problems arise?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning when the 306th Mountain Brigade was formed, there was problems in the Bila Valley, where is where I am from, because at the very beginning one company from Bukovica didn't want to become part of the 306th Mountain Brigade. It became part of the 314th Motorised Brigade; it split off. And later two or three other villages also became part of the 314th Motorised Brigade; they also separated. Some soldiers or some inhabitants become part of the 7th Muslim Brigade and some become part of the 312th Motorised Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, when inhabitants of the Bila Valley joined the various brigades, did this at the time and subsequently create problems for you as the assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: There were quite a few members who joined other brigades. And since they spent their free time in our territory, this caused certain problems and we had no authority over these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, could you now tell me the sort of duties that the security organ of the 306th Mountain Brigade had to perform.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: On the whole, these duties included military police duties, counter-intelligence, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What sort of staff did you in that body have at your disposal? How many of you were there and were these individuals individuals who had previously been engaged in this field of activity?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, in the security organ itself, in the brigade, there was the assistant commander for security and there were two officials; none of them had previously been engaged in that field of activity, apart from the fact that I, when I was appointed to that post, requested a professional, I requested a lawyer. And the official in my service was Haris Jusic, a lawyer, and I think he was of great assistance to me. Whereas, in the battalions there was one assistant commander for security in each battalion, and similarly they didn't have much professional training, but in the 1st Battalion I think the person who had that role had been a professional policeman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, tell me whether in your territory there were individuals -- there were staff who had professional experience but you did not want to engage them, or was the situation such that you had to staff your organ in a certain way?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no such individuals in our territory. Had there been such individuals, we would have gladly engaged them as staff in the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the 306th Mountain Brigade have a military police force? And if so, could you tell me about the strength of that military police force.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: The 306th Mountain Brigade did have a military police detachment. I think there were 28 policemen and one platoon commander, but I'm not sure. But because of the nature, the particular nature of the Mountain Brigade, which was composed of refugees, there was a military police detachment within that unit.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How was your military police platoon organised? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, it was organised so that there were three detachments; two were engaged and one was on leave. As the brigade didn't have sufficient weapons, we had to give some of our weapons to the soldiers at the front lines. So they worked for 14 days and they rested for seven.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the tasks you have mentioned, the tasks that the security organ had to perform, tell me what sort of problems you encountered in the first half of 1993 in your territory. What were the main problems that you had and what were you main tasks?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the main problems and tasks in the first half of 1993 were as follows: The soldiers had not been sufficiently trained and there was a lack of discipline among them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How do you explain those problems? Why were such problems present in your area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, because the local inhabitants lived by raising livestock, by farming the land; so they didn't have any resources, the army couldn't offer them anything. And we couldn't issue them military orders in an effective manner. Everyone wanted to defend his or her own house. So they would refuse to comply with the order to form a brigade on next territorial principle. People searched for food. Soldiers would, as a result, leave the defence lines, they would not respond to the call to man the defence lines. And when a certain number of Arabs arrived in our territory, this compounded the situation. They, these Arabs, went after certain individuals whom they would train. And this resulted in a blockade as well of the territory by the HVO. And our Bila Valley during that period of time was split up into four or five entities. And the command of the brigade itself had been dispersed and consisted of about three entities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Delalic, how did you react to such lack of discipline and what steps did you take against members of the 306th Brigade who were causing you difficulties of this kind?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: At first we would try to talk to them and to persuade the members of the army that they should be disciplined. When those efforts failed, we resorted to military disciplinary measures, reprimands up to detention, and occasionally even criminal reports would be filed against individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Orders were issued to cover those issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The document that you're looking at right now is one -- is it one of those documents whereby the commander was endeavouring to give orders to all soldiers as to how they should behave with respect to civilians and with respect to property?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A moment ago you said that one of the problems that arose in your area, in addition to the numerous units and their members in the area, there was the advent of Arabs. Tell me, when did you notice the presence of those Arabs in your area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I first noted their presence at the end of September, when I joined the Mehurici detachment. We were put up in the elementary school of Mehurici and they were put up in the same school only on a different floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did they stay there for long; and if not, do you know where they went later on?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: With the formation of the 306th Mountain Brigade, the 1st Battalion was given a command post in the Mehurici elementary school; earlier, it was in the elementary school of Visnjevo. So it was moved to the Mehurici elementary school and it stayed there. And with them came a large number of refugees who had no homes and who then became members of our brigade, the 306th. Soon after that, the Arabs moved out to the village of Poljanice or, to be more precise, the Savic houses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, as assistant commander for security of the 306th Brigade, where were you based? Did you remain in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I did not stay in Mehurici; my headquarters were at Rudnik, which is about 6 kilometres from Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me please, what were those Arabs doing when you arrived in Mehurici? And you said it was at the end of September, what were those Arabs doing until the 306th Brigade was formed? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: What I was able to see could be reduced to humanitarian activities among the local population as well as religious teaching of the local population. In that period of time, that was their primary activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As assistant commander for security of the 306th Brigade, did you at any point in time identify any problems that affected the combat readiness of the 306th Brigade and which could be traced to the presence of those foreigners in your area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, because certain members of our brigade would willfully abandon their units and go to be trained by those Arabs. So we couldn't have the necessary personnel we needed for our battalions because fighters were abandoning their ranks, and as a result the commanders were unable to hold the defence lines as required by military principles.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Listing the problems that you were confronted with as the security organ, you said that Arabs tried to win over people. What did they use to do that, to recruit people, which, as you said, could not be mobilised to the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. They had their own methods, but quite a number of people left us for economic reasons. They really didn't have any food at home, and these people provided that food. Another segment was the religious aspect, because some people felt that that was the way they should practice their religion and that is how they won them over.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At some point in time, in addition to this problem of recruitment of the local population, did you discover that those Arabs did something that could be described as a crime?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I was first informed about this while I was at Rudnik, that they had entered the village of Miletici, that is the Arabs had, and that they had committed the act of killing five civilians. And I learned this from Officer Suljic, Dervis. I immediately got in touch with the assistant commander for security of the 1st Battalion, and I ordered him to check out the accuracy of this report and to report back to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When did Dervis Suljic inform you about the event, and did you receive any information from your assistant in the 1st Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection - it was a long time ago - I think Suljic informed us in the morning at the briefing of the brigade command. And at the same time or a little later I was informed by my assistant that a joint commission consisting of members of the 3rd Corps, the HVO, and the international community who were in the area, and that they had established that without any doubt that this had been committed by the Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to the killing of those persons in Miletici, did you receive any information as to what happened to the rest of the inhabitants of that village?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the entire civilian population of Croat ethnicity, and some Bosniaks, too, were taken by them to their camp in the village of Poljanice. My assistant commander for security informed me that with the assistance of the command of the 1st Battalion and also some people of prestige up there, they had been returned to the village of Zagradje and that they were being taken care of by the 306th Motorised Brigade which had a platoon up there that was active against the Chetniks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, did you inform anyone about that event?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I informed, up my chain of command, the organ of military security of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After receiving this information from your assistant for security in the 1st Battalion, first did you have the authority to conduct any additional investigation, or rather, did you have any real ability to undertake anything against those Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I had no authority, especially with respect to the Mujahedin, because they did not belong to the army, and as a result, the situation was extremely complicated on the ground. And with the arrival of the commission, the joint commission consisting of representatives of the HVO and the international community as well, they had no suspicions with respect to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you informed the security organ of the 3rd Corps, did you receive any order to act?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I did receive an order, according to which I should report in greater deal about foreigners as well as about persons who were out of control from our own units and who were sometimes acting together with the Arabs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do after that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 1st Battalion was based in Mehurici, but I also had an assistant commander for security in the 4th Battalion, a part of whose unit was in Mehurici village, and he would come often. And I gave him an assignment to monitor and check the Bosnians who were in that area and who had -- who were out of control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And did you do anything with respect to the Arabs, Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: It was difficult to do anything at all with respect to the Arabs. They never gave their real names; they were mobile; new persons would appear frequently, so that we were unable to do anything in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, regarding the assignment that you received from the security service, did you inform your commander about it and did you try to learn more about those Arabs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I did inform my commander, and we tried to find out more about it. My commander was a professional soldier, and he wanted to learn more about it because this situation affected the combat morale of our units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: The commander offered to join me for us to go and talk to them to see what they actually wanted, and we headed towards the village of Poljanice to talk to these persons. When we reached the entrance to the Mujahid camp there was an obstacle and a guard, I think he was of Arab origin. We stopped and asked to enter. I don't know whether he understood us. In any event, he blew his whistle. And from the first house, as far as I can now remember, two persons came out with arms; one was an Arab and the other appeared to be a local. When they approached us, this local man asked us what we wanted. The commander introduced himself and said that he would like to talk to them about their activities in our area because certain problems were occurring. This person translated this, I assume it was his superior, to his superior, and that one said that they had nothing to discuss with us, that they had seen Mr. Sefer Halilovic and that they were forming the 8th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened then? Were you able to continue this conversation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We could not continue the conversation because they said that they would continue with their efforts to form the 8th Muslim Brigade, which would rely on the supreme command staff. They simply turned around and left us. They were hostile towards us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do after that? Did you inform anyone at all about this?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I informed the superior command of the security service of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, will you now look at the document under tab 10. Could you tell me whether you're familiar with this document.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Who drafted the document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I drafted the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this document are you providing information on the event that you have just described for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did provide such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, in that conversation with the Arabs, were these other individuals mentioned in the document also discussed or is this information that you obtained from some other source?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We didn't speak to them about any other individuals; we didn't have time. And in fact, they didn't make this possible, they wouldn't allow us to do this. And as for other information, I had the Bosnians, I obtained that information through my assistant commander for security of the 1st Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the sake of the transcript, the document we are discussing is DH1007. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you had already received an order to monitor the Arabs in the area and provide information on them, tell me whether up to this event you had this obligation and did you report on what they were doing in that area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, we did have that obligation and we did report on all the information that we obtained through the military security organ. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, when performing your duties as the assistant commander for security, did you find out about any other activities that the Mujahedin were involved in? If that was the case, could you please tell us when and how you came to such information.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, from the end of May 1993 I was at Rudnik at the basic command post there. And I've already mentioned that our command had been dispersed and was in three places. I was there at the command post as the most senior officer in the village near Krpeljici. There was a commander with a chief of staff and two or three assistants of his. And in Mehurici, some of the officers were there. At that time we couldn't establish sufficient command and control over the units. The conditions were not normal for command and control. But from the position at which I was located, I was able to monitor certain events. So towards the end of May, as far as I can remember, the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council, established control over the Bosniak village of Ricice. Inhabitants of that village were ordered to surrender their weapons and to move out. The inhabitants noticed or came to the conclusion that they couldn't defend themselves. They examined the situation and at the time the brigade couldn't help them, and they all moved out, en masse. Then an ultimatum was issued somewhere around the beginning of June. I don't know the exact date, I think it was the 4th of June, an ultimatum was issued to the village of Velika Bukovica in which they were asked to surrender their weapons and to move out; they refused to do so. They did not surrender their weapons and they didn't move out. And on the 6th of June I believe that the HVO attacked the village, and from that area we received alarming information about the vast number of dead and wounded. The most recent information I had during that period was about 18 dead and six wounded. The commander was aware of the situation, and as a reasonable commander, he took certain steps to protect the Bosniak population. He requested assistance from a corps, from UNPROFOR. And from the command post in Mehurici, our units were ordered to lift the blockade of Velika Bukovica. This was difficult. And I think that on the 7th our units didn't believe that it was appropriate to attempt lifting the blockade in Bukovica, but from some telegrams that were sent from the command post to the commander, I could see that the lifting of the blockade of Velika Bukovica was to take place on the 8th of June. That is what in fact took place, and in the morning our unit carried out an attack from the [Realtime transcript read in error "Haric"] Mehurici/Suhi Dol access in the direction of Maline. And by the afternoon they had stabilised the lines behind the village of Maline in the direction of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, tell me, on that day or during the subsequent days, did you find out that in the course of the fighting some events had occurred of interest to security that you were responsible for or with regard to which you took certain measures?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: At the time I was in Rudnik at the command post, at the main command post, and I didn't leave that post. But two or three days later when I went to Mehurici, I found out that a large number of Croatian individuals, Croatian civilians, had been brought in from the village of Maline for their own personal protection because the units couldn't provide them with adequate protection in the village itself. I found out that among these civilians there was some Croatian soldiers, but unfortunately, I also found out that when the column was passing through, 20 civilians were separated, they were singled out, and taken away in an unknown direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What did you do? Did you issue any orders in relation to this event, in relation to the fact that some civilians and soldiers were taken away in an unknown direction; or rather, did you issue any instructions that concerned the HVO soldiers who had been brought in?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as the assistant commander for security for the 1st Battalion is concerned and given that the security organ from the 1st Battalion had been leading a certain group of people from which these individuals had been singled out -- well, I requested this assistant to carry out certain investigations and to determine how this event had occurred. And I issued a task to my officer, Haris Jusic, and asked him to take statements from HVO members. But what we were most interested in at the time were minefields because we had already sustained losses because of their existence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, tell me, did you inform the commander about the information that you had and did you also provide anyone else with the information that you had?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the commander scheduled a meeting for the 12th of June, a meeting of the corps command. At this meeting I provided the information I had obtained, and I said that there were also certain indications according to which people had been killed. I provided the commander with this information and I also provided this information to my superiors in the security corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Have a look at document under number 2, DH1903. Have you had a look at the document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Under tab 2, the document number is DH1903.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the penultimate sentence, it says that "there are indications of the execution of 20 captured civilians and HVO members. Investigation is pending, and upon the completion of the investigation you will be informed on time."

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is this the document in which you provided the 3rd Corps with information of the event?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What was the position of the 3rd Corps command in relation to detecting, investigating, and prosecuting all those who had perpetrated crimes?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, it was clear that it was necessary to investigate such occurrences, and if the perpetrators were identified it was necessary to punish them, if the perpetrators were army members.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, could you please tell me, since you had ordered an investigation to be carried out and you also informed the 3rd Corps of the fact that there was an ongoing investigation, did you find out anything about the results of the investigation and did your assistant for security in the 1st Battalion encounter any difficulties, any problems?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, after about 15 days, as far as I can remember, the assistant commander for security provided me with a report, and all the statements from military police members who had been leading this column were provided to me as well as certain other information. And on the basis of this material, you could see that no one from the 306th participated in those actions, nor had anyone from any other units participated in them. It was quite clear that the Mujahedin unit was responsible for what had been done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform anyone? Did you report to anyone about the information you had obtained in the course of the investigation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I informed my commander and I also informed the superior military security organ.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you found out that it was the Mujahedin who had separated these individuals and taken them away, but probably, as you said, executed certain individuals, did you as the security organ or did your police force carry out an investigation? Were you in a position to carry out an investigation? Or rather, first of all, did you have such authority to investigate the Mujahedin who were not army members and were you in a position to enter the camp and try and investigate the event?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We didn't have the forces required to enter the camp. When you bear in mind how we were received, myself and the commander, it's quite obvious that we could not enter their camp. Had we gone there with the intention of carrying out some sort of an investigation, there would have been an armed conflict, fighting would have broken out, and I didn't have the force for the possibility to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You just mentioned an armed conflict. As the assistant commander for security, did you or was the commander of the 306th Mountain Brigade in -- were you in a position to decide to enter into an armed conflict with individuals who were not army members, in spite of the fact that they were present in your territory? Were you able to make such an assessment and to take a decision on such action?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: No, I couldn't take such a decision. And from my point of view they were more a political problem. It was for someone at the top to deal with this problem. I can now say that, as far as I could see at the time, they were not army members, and by virtue of that fact, I couldn't carry out an investigation into the event.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, what sort of duties did the military police of the 306th Mountain Brigade perform after those events in the month of June? What sort of tasks did it have and what sort of problems did you encounter?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, immediately after those events the military police spent about 20 days at the main command post, which is where it mounted a defence of the main command post. They were quite exhausted. They had been quite traumatised because they had been shelled night and day at the main command post. But in spite of that fact, they immediately started performing their military police tasks. The main objective was to secure the church or the monastery in Guca Gora, the command post, and to an extent their request to participate at the defence lines because the HVO wanted to take back positions that they had lost. So the police were engaged 100 per cent during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It is time for our break. It is half past 10.00 and we will resume at 5 to 11.00. According to my calculations, the Defence has another 25 minutes. We will resume at 5 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. I shall give the floor to the Defence, and looking at the clock, please take note.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, you said that after those combat operations you had a lot to do in view of the situation in the area of the 306th Brigade. Tell me, in connection with the civilian population brought to Mehurici, do you know who took care of that population, who guarded them, and what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the civilian population was taken care of by the civilian community. They were assisted by members of the 1st Battalion. Because they, too, were partly housed in the school, they gave them whatever they could to facilitate their stay there. They also had medical care, they had covers and mattresses, whatever we could give them. And the security was ensured by the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that there were some members of the HVO and that your assistant, Haris Jusic, took statements from them. Tell me, how were those captured soldiers treated and where were they put up?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: They were accommodated in an abandoned smith's, ironsmith's shop. Haris took statements without the presence of the military police. As he was a person -- a civilian, he used to be a lawyer in Nova Bila, and people knew him and we didn't want to frighten people; that's why we chose him. They had three meals a day, they had medical care. The accommodation wasn't too good, but we just didn't have anything better than that to offer them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone complain or did anyone inform you that a member of the army or of the police who was securing them had treated them inhumanely or used cursive measures against them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, no one complained to me. After statements taken, Haris provided those statements to me, and talking to him, as far as I can remember, he also told me that no one had mistreated them in any way.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What happened to those detainees -- or let me ask you first, did any representatives of the International Red Cross come to talk to these people?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the International Red Cross did go to Mehurici. They spoke to those people, but I was not present when they came, as I had other engagements. But my officer, Haris Jusic, was there on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Delalic, what finally happened to those detained members of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We received an order from General Alagic, as far as I can recollect, for them to be escorted to the KP Dom in Zenica. And he mentioned me by name as being held responsible for them. And I thought about the way to transport them to Zenica safely so as to avoid anything that could adversely affect the security situation. So I requested a bus and we transported them by bus to Zenica without any problem.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Look at document number 1, please, it is P104, and tell me, is that the order that you received and which you carried out in the way you have just told us?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I think that it is that order.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the break you spoke about the numerous problems along the lines with the HVO, the duties the military police had with respect to securing the Guca Gora monastery. In that period of time did any other persons or policemen come to assist you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: At the time we lacked the strength to carry out all the planned assignments and -- with our own military policemen. So a squad of the military police battalion from Zenica came to assist us and they secured the monastery at Guca Gora together with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that you said a moment ago that combat operations continued towards the HVO lines, the closeness of front lines, did it affect the ability to preserve the property in the area? Due to combat was any damage inflicted or did you not have any such problems in the area of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: During combat itself, few buildings were damaged. Some were burnt but in small numbers. Probably both sides used incendiary ammunition, but these villages have highly inflammable outhouses, that is haystacks and hay sheds, so once it catches fire, the fire would spread quickly and during the war it was difficult to extinguish such fires. And the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. closeness of the front line led to frequent shelling, particularly around Guca Gora and towards Han Bila, houses were destroyed and set on fire in that way, too.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the area in which you were situated, were there any civilian police stations there and what was their task with respect to the security and safety of people and property in the area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: They also protected civilians to the best of their ability. For a period of time they were resubordinated to us because we didn't have enough strength in view of the breadth of the front line, so we were engaged on the front as well. So I can't remember but they stayed for quite some time in the area. So they cooperated with us as far as they could and as far as the combat operations allowed because the front line was constantly active there, right up until the spring of 1994, that is until the signing of the Washington agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Delalic, in view of the opening of a new front and the lifting of the blockade of the road, did you as the security organ and your military police come across some problems that could not be foreseen or expected?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: All this happened so quickly that we simply could not have foreseen certain things. The opening of the Zenica-Travnik road, which had been blocked, thousands of civilians were moving along that route and various groups of soldiers who could no longer be controlled. I had 29 policemen. If I had had 2.900, I would not have been able to protect each and every individual.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You say you could not have protected every building and every house. Who was living in those houses? What was in danger from those various troops passing there?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Some civilians remained in their houses, but 98, 99 of those houses were abandoned and it was very difficult to control. After combat operations when we were on the defence line, women and children in their hundreds were moving around, looking for food in those houses, and they caused the greatest problems. Then they started taking away furniture and, as winter approached, doors and roof tiles and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to prevent what you have described as looking for food and objects, but in legal terms these would be qualified as theft?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We had very clear-cut positions of the command. Our own positions were clear, too, and we did issue certain orders and instructions. We set up checkpoints, but it's one thing to write something down and another the actual state of affairs on the ground, because there were so many people on the move. And there are -- even if we put a checkpoint at a certain village, there are hundreds of ways getting round it. The military police had markings on them so people knew where they were so people would get round them somehow, and that is how they stole things. But we did what we could in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, you said a moment ago that the superior command had very clear-cut positions. Which command are you referring to with respect to preventing looting and prosecuting perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the superior commands of the 3rd Corps, the operations group, and my own commander of the 306th Brigade. I was saying that positions were quite clear in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of these pronounced difficulties, that it was difficult to control abandoned areas and that villages could be entered from various sides, did you nevertheless manage to identify certain perpetrators and find stolen property? And if so, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We took a series of measures. We would find the perpetrators, we would seize property. If we find someone stealing, we would seize that -- those objects. And then the military police would store those things in certain storehouses near the monastery and the cooperative building in Guca Gora. But those objects were, with time, destroyed, so we couldn't return it to those people except for a man who stayed behind, so we returned to him his passenger car and his tractor. But -- and also in a number of cases we filed criminal reports. But in those days it was very difficult and dangerous to travel to Travnik because the line was constantly exposed to sniper fire, so that in view of that situation, we resorted more to military disciplinary measures, which we proposed to the commander. And I think that we are one of the brigades that issued the largest numbers of decisions regarding detention from 30 to 60 days for such perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you mentioned the burning of houses during combat operations and in the fighting with the HVO until the spring of 1994. Tell me, did you notice any other fires and did you do anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: At one point in time the civil defence informed us that certain Arabs had torched two buildings in Guca Gora. I think we took some statements, but torchings would usually occur at night, when you really were not able to control it. There were also revenge actions. If somebody had someone killed on the front line, he had no other way but to go and set fire to a building at night so that he wouldn't be caught.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, look at document number 5, please. It is number P158. Can you see it? Securing the Guca Gora sector, dated the 16th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This is an order from the 3rd Corps. Is this the order you referred to a moment ago when a part of the military police battalion came to assist you? Were these the assignments you worked on together? Will you now look at the next document, number 6. It is P204.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In this document we can see that Commander Sipic is ordering units of the MUP and the military police to undertake certain measures to prevent looting and torching. You said a moment ago that you set up checkpoints and so on and that all the commands, including your own commander, issued orders. Is this one of those orders which you would issue, or rather, implement as far as possibilities allowed?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me please now, did you continue to have problems with the presence of these Arabs or Mujahedin and did you, as you were duty-bound, inform the command of the 3rd Corps about those problems, or rather, the security organ of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We did continue to have problems. We had a family housed in Guca Gora and they had been threatened. And as we couldn't physically protect them, we brought them there and they lived with us in the monastery. So we protected them in the Guca Gora monastery. We also had a problem that our typist couldn't come to work because she didn't wear a veil and she was not allowed to go to work. And I have a personal example. My daughter had two bullets fired at her because she was not veiled and she was only 15 at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Now, will you look at document 1950 and 1951. Is this the document that you compiled?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There is reference in the document to threats by the Mujahedin against certain Croats, Volic, Zoran; Volic, Davor; and Volic, Vinko. And attached are statements from those persons. Is this something that you informed the military security organ about, that is, the event you mentioned that afterwards you took care of those people in the monastery itself?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is a document referring to that incident about which I informed the superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at document at tab 15. The number of the document is 1400. Is this a document in which you describe and inform the security organ about what happened to your typist?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, although you provided all these reports, during this period of time when you provided such reports, were you able to take any measures against those Arabs, the Mujahedin, or was the situation that you've already described to us such that they were out of the control of the 306th and the ABiH and did that situation continue?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, there was nothing we could do against them. I think that the issue was a political one and someone at the top should have dealt with it, because they informed us that they were negotiating or speaking to someone. They weren't under our control and, as a result, we had no authority over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you were a security officer and, after all, you did speak to the people and you could have certain information about the influence they had on certain people, could you tell me, did you try to assess what an armed conflict with the Mujahedin might result in? How would the local population have reacted?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, they had a significant influence on the local population and I think that the local population would have had a negative relation to the army if we had tried to engage in armed conflict with them at the time, but we really didn't have the forces for such conflict because two fronts had been opened at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time did you try to determine whether an armed conflict with the Mujahedin might also lead to an armed conflict with the population, or rather, even -- or rather, would it have caused certain problems in certain divisions in the units themselves?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of our assessments because while they were present up there they established relations with a lot of families, you know, and it was no longer possible to know whether someone would have obeyed an order to act against them at the time. That is why at that time there was really no possibility to engage in an armed conflict with them and place them under our control.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time did you manage to infiltrate associates of yours among their ranks and were you able to determine the strength of that unit, the number of men they had, the quantity of weapons they had, and the forces that they had?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, in order to infiltrate associates -- you can have three kinds of associates, you know: You can have an economic associate, a patriotic one, and an associate involved in compromising material. But I didn't have any compromising material, I didn't have economic grounds because they never used their real names; they adopted false names. So it really wasn't possible for us to infiltrate any of our associates. But the men who were with them, well, they really didn't want to discuss those matters. It was impossible for us to obtain certain information. We made assessments on the basis of what we could observe. We believed that there was about one battalion present in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to point out to the Defence that your time is up. If you have a final question to put to the witness, go ahead, but please be brief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Did you also provide information to the security organ of the 3rd Corps about your assessments?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I provided all the information I obtained to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the last question is: Have a look at document number 17 and could you tell me whether this is the -- a document in which you found out from the civilian protection that two houses in Guca Gora had been set on fire by the Mujahedin? The number of this document is 1411.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, thank you for your understanding. This concludes my examination-in-chief of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Does the other Defence team have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We only have one question for this witness in order to clarify the transcript on page 26, line 22, 23, 24. In the transcript, it says that: "Units on the 8th of June in the early morning hours set out from the direction of Haric and Suhi Dol, whereas I think that the witness said Mehurici and Suhi Dol in the direction of Maline."

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Is that correct, Mr. Delalic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the units set off from the direction of Mehurici and Suhi Dol.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that at 5.00 in the afternoon the lines were stabilised behind the village of Maline in the direction of Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: Those were the units of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, we have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution. You have one hour and 15 minutes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Delalic. My name is Daryl Mundis --

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My name is Daryl Mundis, and along with my colleagues here, we represent the Prosecution in this case, and I have a few questions to ask you about the matters we've been discussing this morning. Before I do that, though, sir, I would just like to inform you that it is not my intention in any way to confuse you, and I would ask you, sir, that if you don't understand my question, just say so and I'll reformulate or rephrase the question so that you do understand it. Sir, can you tell us to the best of your recollection the date that you assumed responsibilities as the 306th Mountain Brigade assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, from the very beginning of the brigade. It was established on the 22nd of December, 1992, and as of that time I was the assistant commander for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you've told us that you were actually based in Rudnik. Can you confirm for us that at no point in time in 1993 were you actually based in the Mehurici primary school?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that. From the time when the brigade was formed, I immediately went to Rudnik and that's where I was based.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, how long did you remain as the assistant commander for security of the 306th Mountain Brigade? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I remained there until the 14th of February, 1996, and that's when I requested to be demobilised from the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, during the period from 22 December 1992 through the end of 1993 how frequently in the course of your duties you went to the primary school in Mehurici.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I occasionally went there. I had three battalions, and if time allowed this, I wanted to see assistant commanders for security but I was frequently absent and at forward command posts. So I spent quite a lot of time there; sometimes seven days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you be -- you were asked this morning by my learned colleague about the Arabs that were in the school. Do you recall, sir, an approximate month or time period when you became aware that they left the school?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but when the brigade was formed and when the 1st Battalion was deployed in the primary school in Mehurici, soon afterwards they left that place. Perhaps it was a few days later because a certain number of men arrived with the battalion and they had no other accommodation. They had to stay and live in the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I was hoping, sir, that you could be a little more specific. When you say "a few days later," when did the 1st Battalion deploy to the school?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, as soon as the brigade was formed they were given a headquarters in the primary school in Mehurici. So it wasn't possible immediately on the 22nd to move in there, it took perhaps four or five days to move in. I can't remember exactly now, a lot of time has passed and I didn't pay that much attention to the time when they were to move out. During that period of time, we didn't have significant problems that would have led me to monitor them or to pay attention to that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When -- since you say "we didn't have significant problems," when did the presence of these foreigners first become a significant problem, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, it became a significant problem when the events in Miletici occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, that you had three battalions -- or within the 306th Mountain Brigade there were three battalions. I believe also, though, you've made reference, at least in the English transcript, to the 4th Battalion. Were there three battalions or four battalions in the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: In fact there were four battalions; it was a slip of the tongue. Because the brigade was transformed into a light brigade later on and then it was transformed into a mountain brigade again. And later -- and there were three battalions in that unit. At the beginning, initially, there were four battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did each of those battalions have an assistant commander for security? And if so, can you tell us the names of the battalion assistant commanders for security?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Each battalion had such commander. In the 4th Battalion, the commander was Hrustan Zelkanovic; in the 2nd Battalion the commander was Nedzad Begic -- where in fact in the 3rd Battalion the commander was Nedzad Begic; in the 2nd Battalion the commander was Zrakan Husic [phoen]. And Zukanovic Hasan was in the 1st Battalion. They were the assistant commanders for security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, earlier today you've told us about the time in May 1993 where you went with your commander to the Poljanice camp. Can you describe for us this camp or this -- you've also said it was the Savic houses. Can you describe for us what this compound looked like.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I know that place. The houses are on -- are in a field above Mehurici, perhaps about 500 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many houses?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: At the entrance where they lived there were two houses, as far as I can remember, and they had constructed a sort of temporary hut for themselves. Above those houses, about 100 metres away, there was another house. And across the road toward the east there was another house, but I don't know who lived there. I never went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So in this compound, or camp, there were two houses and a hut. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I can remember, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately -- if you're able to tell us, sir, approximately how many square metres was this area?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't understand the question but -- well, perhaps about 20 dulums.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what a dulum is?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: A dulum is 1.000 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, on this occasion in May 1993 when you were at the -- at this location with your commander, you told us you saw a guard who blew a whistle, and then two individuals came out and spoke with you. Other than these three people, did you recall seeing anyone else inside this compound?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't recall having seen anyone else there at the time, but there were probably others there. There were probably people there. But at that point in time two individuals came out when he whistled, and as I have said, one was an Arab and the other was probably a local person, judging by his appearance, and he spoke the Bosnian language very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, this morning you said - and this is reflected at page 24, line 11, of the transcript: "There were persons from our units who were acting together with the Arabs." How many such people, to your knowledge, how many local people, Bosniaks, were acting together with the Arabs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I can't remember exactly whether I said that they cooperated with the Arabs, but they were drawn to them and went to attend training by the Arabs, a part of the local population. In my estimate, from the area of Mehurici there may have been 40 to 50 Bosniaks who were present among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, if you at any point as part of your duties came to know the identity of any of the Bosniaks among these 40 to 50 persons?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Off hand I can't remember, but there were quite a number of criminal reports that we filed against those people. And it was our view that the court would respond. However, as far as I know, the court did not do much with those cases. I don't know what happened later. Some returned to join our units and stayed with the units until the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, when you say "criminal reports were filed," do you know in which court such criminal reports would have eventually landed or ended up at?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Attached to the military prosecutor's office in the court in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of crimes were covered in these criminal reports that you submitted?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: The criminal reports were filed for the act of desertion; willful abandoning of units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you were shown a document, and it's tab 10, which you might want to turn to in the tab -- or in the binder that's before you. At tab 10, this document is DH1007. Do you remember this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: If you look approximately halfway down the document on the left-hand side in the Bosnian version, you'll see two names; Ramo Durmis and Sljivo Malik. Do you see that part of the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the sentence in which their names appear says: "There are a lot of Bosnians with the Mujahedins, who are commanded by Ramo Durmis, and Sljivo Malik is also with him, who used to study in Saudi Arabia." Where did you get this information from, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I got this information from the assistant commander of the 4th Battalion, Hrustan Zelkanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, do you know either of these two Bosniaks who are mentioned in your report?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you, sir, while you've got the binder in front of you and open, if you could turn to tab 15, which is Defence number 1400. And again, my learned colleague from the Defence asked you about this document. And in this daily report that you submitted, it describes the incident involving Zuhra Aganovic, who was a typist. And the English version of this document says: "On 20 August 1993, in the vicinity of the Command of the 306th Mountain Brigade, a group of Mujahedins stopped one of he female employees, Zuhra Aganovic, a typist, on her way to the kitchen for lunch." Can you recall this incident, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I do remember this incident, but I did not draft this document. I wasn't there at the time but I am familiar with the incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit more about the incident? And I'm particularly interested to know where this incident took place.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I can't really read this document well, but this happened somewhere close to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was it in a building? Was it on the street?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: It was outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this kitchen that's referred to in the document, where is this kitchen?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I can't say exactly now because we moved from one command post to another within a brief interval and the kitchens or canteens were in the command premises. But occasionally typists would go to the logistics department, which was outside the command post, and probably as she was went out and was coming back, this happened, because the roads linked Mehurici-Travnik or Han Bila-Travnik, those were the roads there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at any point in time in fulfilling your duties as the assistant commander for security in the 306th Mountain Brigade, did you become aware of the names of any of the Arabs that were in the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: It was very hard to find out their real names. We couldn't get hold of their passports, you see; that's number one. Number two, they would call themselves by names they used, like pseudonyms. They were constantly on the move, new faces kept cropping up, so we simply were unable to discover their proper names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you become aware of any of their pseudonyms or nicknames?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I remember Abu Minaj, for instance. Abu Minaj, that was a nickname, and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where was this Abu Minaj person?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: He was in the initial period in Mehurici in the Savic houses. As far as I was able to find out, that is where he lived, but we didn't know anything more about him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, how did you find out this person's name and the fact that he was one of the inhabitants in the Savici settlement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Passing through Mehurici I would frequently meet with my security officer Zelkanovic, who I said had the duty to sort of monitor things as much as he could. And they would call out to one another using those nicknames, and that is how I memorised this one. And he told me about him, but we didn't know anything more than that about him. They would mostly move from the Savic houses towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how did they move?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: They were motorised. They had Toyotas, they had quite a number of motorcars, and various types of vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than this Abu Minaj, do you remember the names of any of the other Arabs that were in the 306th Mountain Brigade's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember. It really was a long time ago, but I somehow managed to remember this one. Because of the word Abu Minaj, and in our language "mina" means "mine," so it has stuck in my memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, one of the other documents you were shown this morning, which is behind tab 13 and which is 1951, mentions the name Hamza. Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph, right under the line that says: "Today at 1400 hours..."

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I see 2240 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It's the second paragraph. 2240 is the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you know anything about this person, Hamza?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't. I know that after the war there was some problems and that the international police was searching for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn next, sir, to the events in Miletici. You told us, sir, that after they were released from the Poljanice or Savici settlement, the villagers from Miletici were taken to Zagradje. Did you direct any of the personnel in the 306th Mountain Brigade security service to go and interview or speak to the villagers from Miletici in Zagradje?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I said that I gave an assignment to the security officer of the 1st Battalion to go there and to brief me about the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: My question, sir, is a little bit different and it had to go to do not with just going there but my question was: Did you order that security officer of the 1st Battalion to interview any of those Miletici villagers who were accommodated in Zagradje?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the very fact that I sent him there means I ordered him to go there. I didn't order him to interview people, but he knew that they were there and he knew that there was a commission on which there was a representative of the 3rd Corps, of the HVO, and the international community. And they gave their opinion, and on the basis of that opinion he passed on the necessary information to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, do you recall the names of the people who were part of that commission?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I only know that on behalf of the 3rd Corps I think it was Mr. Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever speak to any members of that commission about the events in Miletici?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, following Miletici, you've told us that you considered the Mujahedin to be a significant problem. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And at that point in time, the end of April 1993, you were certainly aware that they were in the camp in Poljanice. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And clearly you knew that they were dangerous, based on the events in Miletici.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, you also testified earlier that they presented a threat to the 306th Mountain Brigade in the sense that they were luring local young men to come and join them, and that would have a detrimental effect on the combat readiness of your brigade. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, the personnel within your security service of the 306th Mountain Brigade would have been aware of these facts as well, would they not?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: They did know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you issue any orders to the members of your security service to avoid the Poljanice camp?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We didn't issue written orders, but orally we did. We spoke about this and said that they shouldn't go there, they couldn't socialise with them, and that they should tell people not to join their units, because they were needed by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell me, sir, why a column of civilians and surrendered HVO soldiers under escort by military police officers of the 306th Mountain Brigade would be marched adjacent to this camp, in light of the information which you've just told us about?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the army couldn't provide adequate protection for the population in Maline, they couldn't remain in Maline. They took them to a safe place in Mehurici. However, this unforeseen, unexpected, incident occurred. No one had expected such a thing. And, you know, at the time I really wasn't in the area; I was in Rudnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, you've told us that you were aware that -- or you've told us that the Mujahedin murdered five villagers in Miletici. You've told us that they were dangerous. You've told us that you ordered your military policemen to stay away from that camp, yet they marched a column of civilians and surrendered HVO soldiers, whom it was their duty to protect, right next to that camp.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: They did lead the column, but it wasn't by the camp. You know they passed eastwards of the camp, you know, somewhere in the area of Maline above Sedici and towards Mehurici.
