And at the time the military police, as far as I can remember, there were about five military policemen, and they really couldn't do anything. The other force was more significant. They were surprised and they took these people from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you just said, "They did lead the column, but it wasn't by the camp." How close did that column get to the Savici settlement?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I can't say for sure the camp, as far as I remember, as far as I know - at the time I wasn't there, as I said. The camp is west of Mehurici and the column passed by to the east of the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How close were they to the camp when the Mujahedin approached the column, based on the information you received from your military police officers?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, they waited for them in the forest. They came out of the forest and took them by surprise. It wasn't in the camp, it wasn't by the camp, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, did you debrief -- did you personally debrief or speak to the military police officers who had been escorting that column?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't speak to them. I let the security officer do that. He was their immediate superior and he reported to me and informed me of all the events, of the conversations he had, of the statements made by those policemen and of any other information he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, you also told us this morning that in the period around the 8th to the 10th, 12th of June, 1993, there was a number of activities undertaken with respect to clearing minefields. Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What unit or units were involved in this mine-clearing operation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: There were engineer units from the 306th Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there soldiers of any unit other than the 306th Mountain Brigade involved in mine clearing in the area around Mehurici and its environs?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, at the time there were no other units involved. According to the information we had on the minefields -- well, this information was provided to battalion commanders and to the chief of the engineer units. And they were involved in clearing those minefields.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me turn now, sir, to the issue of persons who were detained in Mehurici. You told us, sir, that although you didn't personally see it you were made aware that the International Committee of the Red Cross visited Mehurici. And my question, sir, is: Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: When I went to see my official at the time, at that time he told me that the Red Cross had been there and that they had visited these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you say, sir, "my official at the time," are you referring to Haris Jusic?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, during what period Haris Jusic was involved in interviewing or dealing with the HVO soldiers detained in the blacksmith's shop in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: When I arrived in Mehurici, which was about the 11th, I found Haris in Pode, and that's where he was during the blockade of the area. And I assigned him the task of taking statements if there were any interesting questions, and minefields were interesting questions. He immediately started carrying out this task. He took statements in the school, in the office, not in the place you mentioned. We didn't use a single policeman. We didn't want to frighten the people. Haris was a respected lawyer in his company. Many people knew him, and that's why I wanted him to do this, to make sure that no one was frightened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, Mr. Jusic, was he tasked by you with questioning the HVO soldiers or the Croat civilians or both?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Only the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you told us, sir, that those HVO soldiers were being kept in the blacksmith's shop; but, based on this answer, they would then be taken to a room in the school where he would question them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were interviewed in the office in the primary school, but they were being held in the blacksmith's shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, did Mr. Jusic report back to you concerning how this questioning process was going?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, he did report back to me, and I went there myself to see whether this order was being carrying out. And perhaps I would spend four or five minutes there -- perhaps I spent four or five minutes there while a man was being interviewed. The man was smoking a cigarette and speaking quite normally to Haris because he was close to Haris's house, you know, he lived close to Haris's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us during what time period Mr. Jusic was conducting these interviews?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I can't provide you with a precise date, but as I said I arrived there around the 11th and that's when it started. As to when he completed the task, I really couldn't say now. I haven't seen those documents and a lot of time has passed since then, you know, and one forgets things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, how many HVO soldiers were kept in the blacksmith's shop in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly. I don't have the list at the moment, but as far as I can remember, I think there were about 20 or 30 people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir -- I know you said you can't provide a precise date, but a rough approximation how long it took Mr. Jusic to interview these 20 or 30 people? Was it a week? Was it an afternoon? Was it a month?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, it went on for perhaps about seven to ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than Mr. Jusic, were there any other members of the 3rd Corps or any of its subordinate units involved in questioning these 20 to 30 HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, no. Only authorised individuals could enter the premises. As far as I know, Haris said that no one went there. He was the only person present in the course of these interviews.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, with respect to property that was damaged during the course of the war, you told us that a lot of the fires were caused either by shelling or incendiary rounds and consequently were just a result of combat operations. My question to you, sir, is: Did you receive any reports or have any information about fires being intentionally set by members of the 306th Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't have any such information. As I have said, a small number of buildings caught fire in the course of combat. Incendiary ammunition was probably used by both sides. Afterwards, certain buildings were set on fire. I assume that this was also a matter of retaliation. You know that at the lines of defence people were killed, and if someone wants to take revenge, the only way to do so is to set fire to that person's house, you know. And this would usually take place in the evening. Buildings on the other side were frequently destroyed and set on fire when shelling was ongoing. And this was particularly the case in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I take it, then, sir, from your answer that you do not recall any criminal reports being submitted concerning arson or intentional burning of buildings within the 306th Mountain Brigade's area of responsibility? No reports about soldiers being involved in that type of activity?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I didn't say -- well, I said there was certain assumptions. I had a report from the field, from the civilian protection, according to which they had seen certain individuals, certain Arabs, who had set fire to buildings. Someone who wants to set fire to something takes care to hide their traces. I didn't have sufficient forces to prevent such acts. The Bila Valley is a fairly vast area and instead of having -- I would have had to have 2.900 policemen, and not 29, had I wanted to secure each and every building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I understand that, sir, but I'm going to ask the question one more time. My question concerns whether or not you ever saw or were aware of any criminal reports filed with the courts concerning the offence of arson or unlawful burning committed by soldiers of the 306th Mountain Brigade within that brigade's area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: There weren't such criminal reports filed. We did file some criminal reports for theft, but I said that the road to Travnik wasn't very passable. And the courts weren't very up-to-date at the time, so we took disciplinary measures. Usually we would hand down a prison sentence of 30 to 60 days and this sentence would be signed by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, where were these prison sentences carried out?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: The prison sentences that we put into force were put into force within the command. We had a detention unit there and individuals against whom military disciplinary measures were to be taken, individuals who were to serve a 30- to 60-day sentence would serve their sentence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was this detention unit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the detention unit was on the grounds of the monastery. There's a separate building. On the floor there was the military police and on the ground floor there was the detention unit I have referred to. And when we moved from the Guca Gora monastery to the Guca Gora primary school, it was then in a house near the command, that's where the detention unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, sir, if you can help us out: In the Bila Valley, what type of construction material was used in building houses?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Usually bricks were used or blocks, construction blocks. There were quite a few houses built of wood and a sort of earth compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, I believe earlier today you mentioned at some point in time, due to the combat requirements and the need for the military police of your brigade to be involved in certain operations, that the civilian police were resubordinated to your brigade, to the military police of your brigade. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I said that it was resubordinated for a while and it was at a position for about a month or a month and a half in the area of Busjevo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: This was after the combat operations, maybe a month after that. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, in the context of securing the Guca Gora monastery, you told us that it was secured by the military police of the 306th Mountain Brigade as well as some assistance received by members of the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, at any point in time in 1993, did you ever complain to the 3rd Corps about the behaviour of members of the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I think I did, but I didn't complain about security of the building but because of stealing, I think it was cigarettes, from some civilians, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was it -- was this the only instance where you raised a complaint about the behaviour of the 3rd Corps Military Police Battalion, or were there any other instances?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, that was the only occasion when I complained about the behaviour of the police. I was complaining about that squad attached to us, and I asked them to send us another one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately when that was?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us approximately when the military police from the 3rd Corps MP Battalion arrived to assist with securing the Guca Gora monastery?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, immediately after the battles. You see, there was some problems. The military police of the 306th Brigade was stretched too much. We physically were unable to secure everything we should have secured. So they came immediately, as far as I can remember, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and they started to secure with us the actual monastery at Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, sir, when did the military police of the 306th Mountain Brigade begin securing the Guca Gora monastery? On what day?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly, but I know that while I was still at Rudnik I was asked to send a part of the military police over there to protect the monastery. But the command of the 3rd Corps had already taken some steps in that direction and there were police from the 3rd Corps. I said that the system of control and command wasn't functioning well at the time. We wouldn't see or hear one another for a month, me and the commander, we could just talk over the radio and through communications, but it wasn't sufficient for us to deal with everything properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, who asked you to send part of the military police to protect the monastery?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I remember it was my Commander Sipic who was on the ground there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And finally, sir, with respect to a civilian family in the Guca Gora area, you said that in order to protect them, that this family - and the English transcript says - "lived with us in the monastery." This is page 39, line 25. My question, sir, is: Did you personally stay in the monastery for a period of time; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did stay in the monastery. That is where I slept and our command was there, too. Now, I can't recollect exactly when those people arrived, but I think there is an official note saying when they were at risk and then we offered them this. I knew them from before the war, this person, and we are still good friends even after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sir, my question is: When were you and your command housed in the monastery? During what period of time were you personally and the command of the 306th Mountain Brigade present in the Guca Gora monastery?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, maybe about a month, up to two months. We stayed at Krpeljici, that is where the command was, and then to protect the Guca Gora monastery as well as possible, we moved into the monastery itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, I understand, sir, that a dozen years have passed. Can you give us a rough approximation of the time periods when you were at the Guca Gora monastery?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, let's say to the best of my recollection from -- well, from about August 1993 up until the end of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution has no more questions for the witness at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis. It is half past 12.00. We will have the break and after that I will give the floor to the Defence for re-examination. We will resume work at about 5 to 1.00 and we will have three-quarters of an hour available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume. It's 12.56 and I give the floor to the Defence for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we put the ELMO down. Could we move the ELMO a bit because I can't see the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Usher, could you move the ELMO a little.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Delalic, on page 54, lines 5 to 9, you spoke about how at one point in time you realised that the Arabs, or rather, the Mujahedin posed a certain problem because they were trying to lure people. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you started to perceive them as a threat after the events in Miletici. That's your testimony so far. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me, Mr. Delalic, at that time were there any direct attacks carried out by those Arabs against ABiH units, or are these assessments that you made on the basis of the facts that you have already mentioned in the course of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, prior to the events in Miletici, as far as I can remember there were no attacks. But the fact that they were luring our people, trying to entice them to join them for training, shows that they were preparing something that we should have been afraid of. And it is in that sense that I meant that a certain threat was posed by them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague asked you whether you informed your soldiers of this fact, and you said that they were needed by the army and that they should avoid them.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that they were needed by the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when your members of the military police department were taking these people from Maline to Mehurici, tell me, do you think that they could have in any way foreseen such an event? Could they have expected that they might be attacked as they were armed members of the ABiH? Did they act carelessly or were they convinced that they would be able to take these people to Mehurici in safety?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that they were aware of the fact that something like that could happen. They would have probably taken other action at that time in order to reach Mehurici in safety. As I said, they were taken by surprise. They couldn't resist a certain group, and what happened happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from my colleague concerning the billeting of some soldiers in the blacksmith's shop, or rather, concerning the fact that some people were held in the blacksmith's shop, tell me, who secured the blacksmith's shop, which is where these HVO members were being kept at that time?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the civilian authorities secured the premises. The civilian MUP, the civilian police station provided security for the blacksmith's shop through the entire period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did your officer, Jusic, tell you who was bringing those people from the blacksmith's shop to him, and did those people complain about the way they were treated by those who took them from the blacksmith's shop to the school, which is where statements were taken from them?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, they were escorted by the civilian police, but the police only accompanied them to ensure that they were secured. But as far as I know, as far as I was informed, no one complained about receiving threats or about being treated in an inhumane manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that they were given three meals a day. Tell me, at the time how many meals a day were given to army members? And as far as the quality and quantity of the food is concerned, I'm referring to the food given to the prisoners, was the quality and quantity of the food they received different from the quality and quantity of the food given to the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, they received the same food that the troops had. The food was of the same quality as the food given to the troops.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have said that you obtained buses and by order from Commander Alagic you transported these individuals to the KP Dom. While you were taking the HVO members there, did anyone complain to you about being mistreated in any way while in Mehurici?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I assessed the situation and I believe that I was ordered to march the prisoners to the KP Dom in Zenica, but I believed it would be safer to transport them by bus. I asked for a bus and I got one. When I arrived in Mehurici with the bus, as far as I can remember the driver was Enver Gopo [phoen], he was the bus driver. When I arrived there I asked the commander for security, Zukanovic, he came to see me, we put the people on the bus. I asked whether there were any problems and no one complained to me. And I transported them then to Zenica in safety.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have answered my next question. Since you recognised the order that was issued to you, the order which stated that these people should be marched to Zenica, and you have just said that for security reasons you decided to act independently and to act in a way that was in the interest of those prisoners. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I had to take a route that is visible from --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, we've endeavoured to give a little bit of leeway here, but I believe we've gone past the scope of questions concerning or that arise out of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's for you to assess the questions that concerned the prisoners in Mehurici and the way in which they were treated. And I believe that any questions that concern this matter followed in the scope of cross-examination. If you believe that it does not fall within the scope of cross-examination, I will move on to another subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you rephrase the question that you would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, you've just testified that you decided to act contrary to the order, and was this a result of the fact that you wanted to transport these prisoners to the KP Dom under favourable conditions?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one reason. There are people who were 40 or 50 years old and Zenica is quite far from Mehurici and the road itself wasn't safe because it was constantly exposed to fire from the HVO lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from my learned colleague when you were asked to describe the Savica Kuce, the Savica houses place, you said that you were familiar with that place. Please tell me, how long had you been familiar with the area around the Savica houses?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I was born perhaps 2 or 3 kilometres from the Savica houses, to the west, to the Vlasic Mountain. I hadn't visited that property but when going from my village to Mehurici it can be seen, you can see Savica Kuce on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In the course of 1993 when the Mujahedin made their -- set up camp there, did you ever enter the premises of the camp, apart from the time when you arrived before the camp with the commander?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: The only time I went there was when I went there with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Perhaps my question was not interpreted quite correctly. I asked whether the witness had ever in the course of 1993, that is to say while the Mujahedin were present there, entered the camp. And my colleague has said that the question is not precise, but I think the witness understood my question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague asked you a number of questions that concerned houses being set on fire, and you said that that usually took place at night, that you had information from the civilian protection according to which the Mujahedin had set fire to two houses. In the course of your investigations, patrols, or when other police organs went on patrol, did they ever detect members of the 306th Brigade engaged in setting fire to houses?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: We never found any members who set fire to the houses, but we did find members who were engaged in looting. And as I have said, we would confiscate those houses. We filed a certain number of criminal reports with regard to these thefts but mostly we would take disciplinary measures against those perpetrators and they would be given a 30- to 60-day prison sentence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question from my learned colleague you repeated what you already said and when I asked you. You said that even if you 2.900 policemen and not just 29 policemen it would have been difficult to secure each and every abandoned house. Tell me, did certain organs nevertheless, once they realised the scale of the problem, take certain measures in order to protect their property?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I know, the civilian organs, the civilian authorities, civilian protection started taking certain steps. They moved refugees into these houses and, as far as I understood, this was the best possible protection for such property. Certain parcels of land were distributed so the people could work the land and survive. And wherever people moved in, whenever refugees were expelled, people moved into the houses, the houses were protected and there were no problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Page 64 lines 5 to 6, when responding to a question put to you by my learned colleague, you said that at one point in time, and you tried to be more precise later on, you said that it was in August 1993 the command of the 306th Brigade moved into the Guca Gora monastery. Tell me, what was the main reason for which the command decided to move into the monastery?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what guided the commander when he decided to move there, when he decided to go there. But later we realised that that was the best course to take in order to provide the best possible protection for the monastery and in order to be able to provide protection for the books in the monastery and everything around the monastery. In order to be able to do this, we moved into the monastery.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, tell me, that since the monastery also had a church and a number of buildings, this is what we have heard from other witnesses, at least, tell me whether the command was in the church or in one of the buildings on the grounds.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I'd never been in the church before that time. I don't know whether the church is the part where religious rites are performed. You know, where we were in the premises where the nuns and the fathers slept; that's where we were and that's where we had our offices. In another building, separated from the one we were in, there were the military police, and down below we had the detention unit for members of the military.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Delalic, please tell me, since you said that you were there in order to protect the building, what was the attitude of the army and the command to everything on the compound? You mentioned books. Were they protected? What was your attitude towards the collection of books in the monastery? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, when we arrived there I must say that in the course of the fighting and everything else, someone probably requested certain books. As far as I can remember, the books weren't in order. The library was a nice one, and I as a graphic designer, someone involved in the printing of books, I made an effort and I think the entire command did so, too, we made an effort to protect what had remained there, to take care of this collection, and we didn't let anyone from that point in time touch those books.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: First tell me, who did you hand the monastery over to?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I think that we handed the monastery over to the religious authorities when an order was issued according to which we were to move into it. We then moved into the primary school in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, if you were present when the monastery was handed over to them, did these members of the clergy state what their position was with regard to the fact that the monastery had been protected and preserved in those very difficult times?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't present at the time. As I have said, I was frequently absent; I was at the front lines, facing the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressor. I would often be absent for seven days and sometimes even longer, but I did have the opportunity of getting to know a guardian who was there. I spoke to him, I can't remember his name now, but he was content with what we had done. At least, that's what he said; we protected everything that could have been protected after that fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 61, lines 15 and 16, in response to a question from my learned colleague about resubordinating part of the civilian police to the 306th Brigade, you responded to this question, but can you tell me, who took the decision that a unit of the civilian police should be resubordinated to the 306th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation in the field was such that our soldiers were exhausted. And given the checkpoints and the security we had, the men were very tired. And given their exhaustion, a time arrived when they could no longer continue to perform their duties. As far as I know, the commander requested the MUP to be resubordinated at that time and to be at the defence lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me which police station was resubordinated to you?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: It was the Mehurici police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And tell me whether there were any other police stations, civilian police stations, present in the same area and did they perform their basic police tasks?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, there was the Han Bila station. I don't exactly know how they were organised now. These were certain branches. You know, some of the men from all the stations were resubordinated to us; whereas, others continued to carry out their daily tasks and duties that they had as the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, given the defence tasks that you had and you and the military police -- and the tasks that you and the military police had, tell me, do you know whether at any point in time in 1993 was the situation in which the army took over police tasks or was the police involved in carrying out its tasks throughout that period of time in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Well, if you're referring to the civilian police, the civilian police continued to carry out its work throughout that period of time. The military police didn't meddle -- the military police didn't meddle if the protection of civilians was concerned. There was cooperation, but they never ceased to perform their daily duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to my learned friend, you -- on page 63, line 22, you said that you had a brigade detention unit. Tell me, please, you as the 306th Brigade, did you have a barracks where all the soldiers would be quartered and where there could be a detention unit for a brigade such as yours, or were the fighters living in their own homes?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: The combatants were mostly living at home. We didn't have the necessary preconditions for housing them in barracks. Occasionally we held about a platoon or a smaller unit to faze the Serbian-Montenegrin aggressor when the conditions allowed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to one of the first questions put to you by my learned friend of whether you had three or four battalions, you said that you made a mistake, that at first there were four and later on when you re-organised there were three. Tell me, when did one of the battalions of the 306th Brigade cease to belong to the 306th Brigade and to what unit was it attached and continued to operate, within which other unit?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I did say that. At first we had four battalions and that one of them was called the Sipreski Battalion, consisting of refugees, and it also had a military police squad. I think sometime in August they formed a brigade, the 27th Brigade, and they joined the brigade; whereas, some from the Bila Valley that belonged to the 314th Brigade joined their brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Where was this newly formed brigade based?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: The headquarters of the 27th Brigade was in Mehurici, but not in the school anymore because the school was given to be used for another purpose, but in a house. I think it was Ferid Jasarevic's private house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In connection with these questions, do you know how many 3rd Corps Brigades could be housed in barracks and have appropriate detention units such as the JNA used to have in its day?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a single brigade except perhaps the 17th, because it was a brigade of refugees and I think they lived in barracks. But as for others, while the members were on the front lines, they would be there, and when they were released from the front, they would go to their own homes. We didn't have barracks for accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And my last question, Mr. Delalic, is the following: Answering questions put to you by me and my learned friend you described a number of events from 1993. Could you please tell me how important for your brigade for that whole period was the assignment to hold on to the lines towards the Serbian army while at the same time having to fight the HVO? To what extent was that a priority task above all others?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: It was the absolute priority. Our brigade had one of the largest areas of responsibility on the defence lines, so that we held almost the entire eastern slopes of Mount Vlasic towards the Serbian-Montenegrin aggressor. And then in June 1993 we were given another such zone. Had we failed at one spot, the Bila Valley would have fallen and you know what happens in that case to the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions from us, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I have one question to put to you, only one. That is about the column of persons that were brought from Maline to Mehurici on the 8th of June. You told us about that this morning. You said some 20 to 30 persons were selected from the column and your later investigations revealed that they were taken by the Mujahedin and probably killed by the Mujahedin. Is that a correct summary of what you said this morning?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I said that the military police, consisting of five or six policemen who were escorting that column, was caught by surprise by people with weapons who were very serious and very dangerous, and I said that about 20 people were taken away. According to all information obtained after an investigation, it was established that about 25 people had been executed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: That's right. That's what I wanted to summarise as briefly as adequate, but I totally agree with you that you said so. I have one question on this event. We have heard many other witnesses who said the same thing as you said to us this morning. My question is related to a document that you wrote some months later, in the fall of 1993, and this is also in your binder that you have before you. It is tab 4, and I would like to -- would invite you to take a look at your document that you signed on the 19th of October. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the document. This is your signature, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is not my signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Whose signature is it, then? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I cannot recognise the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: And do you remember the report itself and the content of this report? Please have a look and read it first because otherwise ...

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: All I can say is that I see this document for the first time. I did not compile it and I don't know who may have done it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: So you cannot really comment on the content of the report?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I think that I first informed the superior security organ that there were certain indications, and some 15 days later I confirmed this in a second report, and I said that that was the end of it for me because the Mujahid unit was not within the jurisdiction of the 306th Mountain Brigade. Someone else at the top should have addressed that problem, people that they had negotiated with, so I cannot accept this document. I really don't know who signed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the autumn of 1993 the Operation Group Bosanska Krajina made a request to the 306th Brigade to report on the events of June? Are you familiar with that then?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SWART
utterances.text: Well, then I really suppose you cannot comment on the content. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I am concerned, go back to document number 4. You just said that you don't know who signed the document. Can you please look at the document. To the left there is -- there are initials FO/AZ. We know because other witnesses have told us that the author of the document places his initials and the typist his or her initials. So can you tell us what FO could be in your unit? Because somebody who signs must have the authority to sign.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: In my unit -- in my unit, the initials could be of the clerk Osman Fusko, but I can't recognise his signature. I did not order this, I did not draft it, and I'm really not aware of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're talking about documents. Could you please now look at document number 2 that you have in your binder from the 306th Brigade of the 3rd Corps. Have you found that document?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you tell me, at the bottom to the left in your language, it says "babela 802." What does that mean, "babela 802"?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but this must have been a code name, a secret name for a certain person. And this was the code used in radio communications, or it could have been for a unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we know which unit it is. It is the 306th Brigade which is sending this report to the 3rd Corps. So you're telling us that who drafted this document, you used the code name babela 802. Is that your interpretation?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I'm unable to confirm that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A final question: You spoke a moment ago about the reasons for a fire in houses and you said that both sides had incendiary bullets. To the best of your knowledge, the soldiers of the 3rd Corps in combat operations did have -- did they have incendiary bullets?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, the command during combat operations and distribution of ammunition, they did not distribute such ammunition. But there were fighters who managed to get hold of such ammunition on the black market. And that is how incendiary bullets were used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was an incendiary bullet more expensive than a normal bullet on the black market?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I didn't make any such purchases, so I don't know what the prices were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. Have the Prosecution any questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the Defence? We have seven minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Delalic, His Honour showed you the document number 4 and you said that you could not recognise the signature. As this is the document of the 19th of October, 1993, do you know who was your brigade commander at the time?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recollect, the brigade commander was Vezir Jususpahic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did Mr. Vezir take over as brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date but I think it was sometime in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us for how long Mr. Vezir remained commander of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: For about three or four months, as far as I can recollect.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Around this date, the 10th, were you mostly in the brigade command or did you have other duties within the area of responsibility of your brigade?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: I said before that I had to go to forward command posts so that I was frequently absent, and I really don't know where exactly I was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could the brigade commander ask for information about events that occurred before he came from other members of your body, that is, from other members of the command if he was asked to provide such information? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander could ask for such information, but if I was present, he should have asked me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And if he didn't ask you for such information, does that unless confirm your previous testimony that you were frequently absent from the command?

utterances.speaker: ASIM DELALIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, he didn't ask me ever for this information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Your testimony has just been completed. Thank you for coming to testify in The Hague at the request of the Defence. You have answered all our questions. On behalf of the Chamber, I wish you all the best and a safe journey home, and will Mr. Usher accompany you out. We shall now go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence would like to tender into evidence as Defence exhibits documents under number 13, number 1951; number 14, 1952; number 15, 1400; number 16, 1406; and number 17, 1411. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you please do your duty.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have five documents admitted into evidence as Defence exhibits under the following numbers: DH1952 -- [In English] DH1951, with it's English version DH1951/E. The number 1952 under the reference DH1952, and then the English version DH1952/E. The number DH1400 under the reference DH1400/E -- sorry, DH1400, and the English version DH1400/E. The number 1406 admitted into evidence under DH1406, with an English version DH1406/E. Finally the number 1411 is admitted into evidence under the reference DH1411, with an English version DH1411/E. [Interpretation] I take advantage to make a correction in the transcript regarding the documents admitted this morning. [In English] DH2032 is admitted into evidence and not marked for identification as wrongly indicated on the transcript, with an English version DH2032/E. [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber takes note of these numbers. In the few seconds remaining to us, I invite all the participants, the Prosecution, the Defence attorneys, the accused, and all the personnel of this courtroom to meet again for the hearing which will begin on the 28th of February, Monday, at 2.15 when we will be resuming our public hearings. Thank you all. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 28th day of February, 2005, at 2.15 p.m.
